tier_reason: The README 'Benchmarks' section compares easyjson directly with encoding/json ('standard' rows) in MB/s tables, and the benchmark code is public (benchmark/default_test.go, benchmark/easyjson_test.go, run via make). No CPU model and no Go version or flags are given for the standard/easyjson rows, so it is first-party with partial methodology: tier C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: 'easyjson is roughly 5-6 times faster than the standard encoding/json for unmarshaling, and 3-4 times faster for non-concurrent marshaling. Concurrent marshaling is 6-7x faster if marshaling to a writer' (verbatim from README). Table (MB/s, derived from page data): unmarshal regular 125 vs 22 (~5.7x), small 67 vs 9.7 (~6.9x); one-goroutine marshal regular 213 vs 75 (~2.8x), to a writer 263 vs 75 (~3.5x), small 125 vs 32 (~3.9x), large 212 vs 80 (~2.7x); concurrent marshal regular 792 vs 252 (~3.1x), to a writer 1748 vs 252 (~6.9x), large to a writer 2134 vs 289 (~7.4x)
corrections.caveats: The README does give exact MB/s, allocs/op and B/op tables, not only rounded ranges. No CPU model is stated. The only Go version mentioned is go1.6, and it is attached to the ffjson (2016-02-04) and go/codec (2016-03-04) result runs, so the tables are from 2016 and do not reflect later encoding/json improvements. Non-concurrent marshaling without a writer is ~2.7-2.8x on the regular and large payloads, below the prose '3-4x'. Results use easyjson's default mode, which uses unsafe.

notes: Claim quote is verbatim and matches the README tables. Metadata checks out (MIT, not archived/fork, 4,917 stars, last commit 2026-03-14, active). Go project, not C++.

tier_reason: cpp-serialization-benchmark README runs Cista++ against cereal on the same graph workload with public code (src/main.cc, src/cista.cc, src/cereal.cc, Google Benchmark). It states GCC 11, the Release build type (README build steps), and AMD Ryzen 9 5900X; the raw output is in benchmark_result.txt.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Cista++ `offset` (slim variant) vs cereal: serialize 4 ms vs 216 ms, deserialize 0.16 ms vs 111.00 ms, deserialize & traverse 66 ms vs 174 ms (derived from page data: ~54x, ~690x, ~2.6x); serialized size 25.3M vs 37.8M. Traverse alone is 67 ms for both. Compile time (clang-7 on Mac OS X): Cista++ `raw` 1.351 s vs cereal 1.827 s
corrections.compiler_and_flags: GCC 11, CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release from the README build steps (CMakeLists.txt adds no other optimization flags; C++20); compile-time table uses clang-7 on Mac OS X
corrections.caveats: Benchmark numbers come from felixguendling's own companion repo (cpp-serialization-benchmark), so they are first-party, but methodology (code, compiler, build type, CPU) is public, which is why it qualifies for tier A. The run is from 2021-12-18 (benchmark_result.txt) with Cista pinned as a submodule at d3492bf; the benchmark repo has not changed since 2021-12-31, and that run warns that CPU scaling was enabled. The 1.351 s compile time is for the `raw` variant, and `raw` serializes slower than cereal (650 ms vs 216 ms); the win is for the `offset` slim variant. The main cista README shows an older 2019 run (72 ms vs 239 ms serialize), which points the same direction. The very large deserialize speedup vs cereal is an architectural effect of zero-copy access (no parsing step), not a benchmarking artifact.

notes: Numbers match the Cista++ `offset` row (= cista_offset_slim_bench in benchmark_result.txt); ratios were not marked as derived, now fixed. Compile-time figure belonged to the `raw` row. Metadata correct (MIT, 2,253 stars, last commit 2026-09-25, active).

tier_reason: struct_pack_intro.md charts compare struct_pack with protobuf, msgpack and flatbuffers using public code (src/struct_pack/benchmark/benchmark.cpp, config.hpp: OBJECT_COUNT=20, ITERATIONS=1000000). The page states Alibaba Clang 13 and a Xeon Platinum 8163. Flags come from the committed build config: cmake/build.cmake defaults CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE to Release, matching how earlier verdicts treated a default Release build.

corrections.claimed_speedup: (derived from page data, estimated from the PNG bar charts; each case is a vector of 20 objects) Serialize: struct_pack ~15-20 ns vs protobuf ~325 ns for 20 rect (~16-20x), ~100-110 ns vs ~540 ns for 20 person (~5x), ~665 ns vs ~2,900 ns for 20 monster (~4.4x); msgpack ~1,100-8,000 ns on the same cases. Deserialize: ~210 ns vs protobuf ~1,090 ns (20 rect, ~5x), ~960 ns vs ~2,130 ns (20 person, ~2.2x), ~7,600 ns vs ~17,500 ns (20 monster, ~2.3x). Repo README: '2-20x faster than protobuf'
corrections.workload: Serialize and deserialize vectors of 20 objects of three struct shapes (rect: 4 int32_t; person: int64_t id, std::string name, int age, double salary; nested Monster with strings, vectors and an enum), with pre-initialized objects and pre-allocated buffers, averaged over one million iterations; compared to protobuf, msgpack and flatbuffers (flatbuffers serialize only), using compile-time reflection (no macros for aggregate types)
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Alibaba Clang 13 (stated on the page). Flags are not on the page; cmake/build.cmake defaults CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE to Release (-O3 -DNDEBUG), and the benchmark target defines STRUCT_PACK_OPTIMIZE and MSGPACK_NO_BOOST
corrections.caveats: Numbers are only in PNG bar charts (no text table), so the figures are estimates from the chart axes. Each chart case is a vector of 20 objects. Alibaba Clang 13 is Alibaba's internal Clang build, which limits exact reproduction. The charts were added to the docs on 2023-07-05 and are not tied to a stated commit; the current benchmark.cpp also runs single-object cases and struct_pb. The docs compare against protobuf/msgpack/flatbuffers, not Boost.Serialization or cereal, hence baseline_in_list=false.

notes: Record's person serialize figure (~120 ns, ~4.4x) was slightly off; pixel measurement gives ~100-110 ns vs ~540 ns (~5x). 'Used internally at Alibaba' is not stated in the README or the benchmark page, so it was removed from stars_or_usage. Metadata correct (Apache-2.0, 2,181 stars, last commit 2026-09-21, active).
